summary: Defines enhancements to OSPF to support Opaque LSAs, a new class of link-state advertisement that carries application-specific information through the network. It was replaced by RFC 5250.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF lets routers carry information about the network in link-state advertisements, called LSAs. This RFC adds a kind of LSA whose contents are whatever a particular application wants, so new applications can use OSPF's existing flooding machinery without changing OSPF itself.

subtitle: A way for applications to carry their own information across an OSPF network, using the existing link-state flooding.

tldr.problem: OSPF's link-state advertisements have a fixed set of defined types, so an application that needs to distribute information across an OSPF domain has no agreed way to do it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Opaque LSAs, link-state advertisements of type 9, 10 and 11 whose body is application-specific, and whose type determines whether they are flooded over the local link, across one area, or across the whole autonomous system.
tldr.outcome: Routers can carry application data without changing OSPF, and each router learns from a neighbour's Database Description packets whether that neighbour understands Opaque LSAs. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 5250 and updated by RFC 3630.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
OSPF has been widely deployed throughout the Internet, and as a result it has been extended to support many options; this evolution will obviously continue. This memo defines enhancements to the OSPF protocol to support a new class of link-state advertisements called Opaque LSAs, which provide a generalized mechanism for the future extensibility of OSPF. The information contained in an Opaque LSA may be used directly by OSPF or indirectly by some application wishing to distribute information throughout the OSPF domain, for example the distribution of IP to link-layer address resolution information. The exact use of Opaque LSAs is beyond the scope of the memo.

An Opaque LSA consists of a standard LSA header followed by a 32-bit aligned application-specific information field. Like any other LSA, it uses the link-state database distribution mechanism for flooding this information throughout the topology. The link-state type field of the Opaque LSA identifies the LSA's range of topological distribution, which is called the flooding scope.

The memo envisions that an implementation of the Opaque option provides an application interface for encapsulating application-specific information in a specific Opaque type, for sending and receiving that information, and for informing the application of a change in the validity of previously received information when topological changes are detected.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF lets routers carry information about the network in link-state advertisements, called LSAs. This RFC adds a kind of LSA whose contents are whatever a particular application wants, so new applications can use OSPF's existing flooding machinery without changing OSPF itself.

sections.title: The Opaque LSA and Its Scopes
sections.content:
Opaque LSAs are types 9, 10 and 11 link-state advertisements, and each one is a standard LSA header followed by a 32-bit aligned application-specific information field. The link-state ID of an Opaque LSA is divided into an Opaque type field, the first 8 bits, and a type-specific ID, the remaining 24 bits.

The link-state type gives the flooding scope. A type-9 Opaque LSA has a link-local scope and is not flooded beyond the local subnetwork. A type-10 Opaque LSA has an area-local scope and is not flooded beyond the borders of its associated area. A type-11 Opaque LSA is flooded throughout the Autonomous System, with the same scope as an AS-external type-5 LSA: it is flooded through all transit areas, is not flooded into stub areas from the backbone, and is not originated by routers into their connected stub areas. A type-11 Opaque LSA received in a stub area from a neighbouring router inside that stub area is rejected.

The responsibility for proper handling of the flooding scope is placed on both the sender and the receiver. A receiver must always store a valid received Opaque LSA in its link-state database, and it must not accept Opaque LSAs that violate the flooding scope, such as a type-11 domain-wide Opaque LSA in a stub area. The flooding scope affects both the synchronization of the link-state database and the flooding procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: Three numbers pick how far an Opaque LSA travels: 9 stays on the local link, 10 stays inside its area, 11 crosses the whole routing domain. The link-state ID is split into an 8-bit type that says what the contents mean and a 24-bit identifier.

sections.title: Flooding Opaque LSAs
sections.content:
Flooding follows the OSPF flooding procedure, with type-specific restrictions. A type-9 Opaque LSA must not be flooded out an interface other than the one it was received on, so an implementation should keep track of the IP interface associated with each link-local Opaque LSA. A type-10 Opaque LSA must not be flooded out an interface whose area differs from the area the LSA is associated with, so an implementation should keep track of the OSPF area for each area-local Opaque LSA. A type-11 Opaque LSA must not be flooded out an interface associated with a stub area, and one received on such an interface must be discarded and not acknowledged, because the neighbouring router flooded it in error.

When opaque-capable routers and routers that do not support the option are mixed in a routing domain, the Opaque LSAs are not flooded to the routers that do not understand them. Optional OSPF advertisements are only flooded to the routers that understand them.
sections.plainLanguage: A router keeps each Opaque LSA within its allowed area. If a type-11 advertisement turns up inside a stub area, the router throws it away and does not acknowledge it, because the router that sent it should never have flooded it there.

sections.title: Capability Exchange and the Neighbor State Machine
sections.content:
An opaque-capable router learns of its neighbour's capability at the beginning of the Database Exchange process, when it receives Database Description packets from a neighbour in state ExStart. A neighbour is opaque-capable if and only if it sets the O-bit in the Options field of its Database Description packets; the O-bit is not set in packets of other types. In the next step of the Database Exchange process, Opaque LSAs are included in the Database summary list sent to the neighbour if and only if the neighbour is opaque-capable. When flooding Opaque LSAs to adjacent neighbours, the opaque-capable router checks the neighbour's capability, and Opaque LSAs are placed only on the link-state retransmission lists of opaque-capable neighbours. A non-opaque-capable router that receives one anyway simply discards it as an unknown LSA type.

The neighbour state machine is unchanged except for the action associated with the state ExStart and the event NegotiationDone, which is where the Database summary list is built. The router must list the contents of its entire area link-state database in the neighbour Database summary list: the Router LSAs, Network LSAs, Summary LSAs and types 9 and 10 Opaque LSAs in the area structure, along with AS External and type-11 Opaque LSAs in the global structure. AS External and type-11 Opaque LSAs are omitted from a virtual neighbour's list, and also omitted if the area has been configured as a stub area. Type-9 Opaque LSAs are omitted if the interface associated with the neighbour is not the interface associated with the Opaque LSA.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router says in its Database Description packets whether it understands Opaque LSAs, by setting a bit called the O-bit. Only routers that set that bit are sent Opaque LSAs. When a router builds the summary of its database for a neighbour, it lists the Opaque LSAs that the neighbour's area and interface allow.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
The OSPF MIB provides objects for managing and monitoring a router's link-state database, and the ones relevant to the Opaque option are described. The ospfGeneralGroup defines two objects for keeping track of newly originated and newly received LSAs, ospfOriginateNewLsas and ospfRxNewLsas. The OSPF MIB also defines optional traps: ospfOriginateLsa signifies that a router has originated a new LSA, and ospfMaxAgeLsa signifies that one of the LSAs in the link-state database has aged to MaxAge. The ospfAreaTable describes the configured parameters and cumulative statistics of the router's attached areas, including a count of the LSAs in the area's link-state database and a sum of their checksums, which can be used to detect a change in the database and to compare the databases of two routers. The ospfLsdbTable describes the link-state database excluding AS-external LSAs, with entries indexed by an Area ID, a link-state type, a link-state ID and the originating router's Router ID.

New management objects are needed. An object is needed to indicate whether the Opaque option is enabled on the router, and the origination and reception of new Opaque LSAs should be reflected in the counters, inclusive of types 9, 10 and 11. The number of type-10 Opaque LSAs should be reflected in ospfAreaLsaCount and their checksums included in ospfAreaLsaChksumSum, and type-10 Opaque LSAs should be included in the ospfLsdbTable. Because LSAs have not previously had a link-local scope, a new group of objects is required for type-9 Opaque LSAs: a count, a checksum sum and a table for the type-9 link-state database on a per-interface basis. A similar new group is required for type-11 Opaque LSAs, with a count, a checksum sum and a table for the type-11 link-state database, so that type-11 LSAs can be displayed once for the router rather than once in each non-stub area.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks for a few new SNMP counters and tables so that an operator can see how many Opaque LSAs a router holds, what they are worth, and where they came from. Because type-9 and type-11 LSAs have scopes no earlier LSA had, they need tables of their own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two kinds of issue need addressing when protecting routing protocols from misconfiguration and malicious attack: authentication of the protocol information, and denial of service attacks resulting from repetitive origination of the same router advertisement or from originating a large number of distinct advertisements that overflow the database. Both concerns exist independently of a router's support for the Opaque option.

OSPF protocol exchanges are authenticated. One of the authentication types, the Cryptographic authentication option, appends a message digest to transmitted OSPF packets, and receivers use the shared secret key and the received digest to verify that each packet is authentic. The quality of that protection depends on the strength of the message digest algorithm, MD5 being the only one specified at the time, the strength of the key, and correct implementation in all communicating OSPF implementations. It also requires all parties to keep the shared secret key secret. None of the standard OSPF authentication types provide confidentiality or protect against traffic analysis.

Repetitive origination is handled by OSPF's rule limiting the frequency at which new instances of a particular LSA can be originated and accepted during flooding. The frequency at which new LSA instances may be originated is once every MinLSInterval seconds, whose value is 5 seconds, and the frequency at which they are accepted during flooding is once every MinLSArrival seconds, whose value is 1. When the link-state database becomes very large, routers with limited resources can be accommodated by configuring OSPF stub areas and NSSAs.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding Opaque LSAs does not change OSPF's security story. Packets are authenticated with a shared key and a message digest, and OSPF limits how often the same advertisement can be re-originated, so that a router cannot flood the database by repeating itself.
